section_titles: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
periods.activity_title: Seeing the Same Thing from Different Sides

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the hide-and-seek picture; answer: (a) which game, (b) who looks from top, (c) if Rani faces hut in Scene 1 can she see who is hiding — discuss.
Mini, Bholu and Rani drew the same brick differently — discuss why; fill table: whose drawing shows top view, front view, side view.
Match the side/front/top view drawings made by Jagat and Rani with the correct 3D objects (pyramid, cube, prism/wedge).

homework.description: Look at nine pictures of objects (TV, sofa, slipper, cup, school bus, chair, bolt, pizza cutter, helmet); write each object's name and which view is shown.

time_bands.activity: Students study the hide-and-seek scene and discuss Let Us Do Q1, p.24 ("look at the hide-and-seek picture; answer: (a) which game....") in pairs; the class shares responses, noticing that the viewer's position determines what is visible.

Students examine the three brick drawings and work through Let Us Do Q2, p.25 ("Mini, Bholu and Rani drew the same brick differently — discuss why...."), completing the table that names each child's view. The teacher draws attention to how standing above, in front, or to the side produces a different outline.

Students attempt Let Us Do Q4, p.27 ("match the side/front/top view drawings made by Jagat and Rani with the correct 3D objects...."), matching labelled view drawings to pyramid, cube, and prism shapes. Pairs compare their matches and articulate the reasoning that connects each view to its object.

periods.teacher_notes: Children commonly assume the front view always looks like the object's 'face' regardless of orientation — use the brick task to surface this by rotating a real rectangular box and asking what changes. Let Us Do Q3, p.26 is set as home practice so students can apply view-naming independently to a wider set of objects.
materials: Rectangular box or thick book to demonstrate rotation

section_titles: Boxy Buildings — Building and Drawing Multiple Views
Cat Finds Jagat — Row and Column Positions
periods.activity_title: Build It, Draw It, Find Your Place

tasks_in_class.description: Collect empty matchboxes or boxes; build different buildings; draw their top, side, and front views; challenge friends to match drawing to building.
Mark Jagat's position (3rd desk, 1st row); describe position of blue bag; identify object at middle desk of 2nd row; locate notebook; draw an apple at 3rd desk of 2nd row.

time_bands.activity: Each group receives a handful of empty matchboxes and constructs a small building of their choice, then draws its top view, front view, and side view on grid paper. Groups swap only their drawings (not the structure) and attempt to reconstruct their partner's building — brief sharing reveals how much information three views together carry.

Students open to the classroom grid on page 28. Working through Let Us Do Q1–5, p.28 ("mark Jagat's position (3rd desk, 1st row); describe position of blue bag...."), they mark and name positions using the row-column system, finishing by drawing an apple at the specified desk. The class discusses how 'row' and 'column' give a two-part address for any location on the grid.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical) — use the classroom's own desk arrangement as a live example before students open their books. The Boxy Buildings activity deepens understanding of top, front, and side views established with the brick drawings; draw that connection explicitly by asking students which view is hardest to guess from a drawing alone.

section_titles: Grid Game — Describing Positions on a Grid
periods.activity_title: Place It, Move It — Grids and Treasure Paths

tasks_in_class.description: Fill Bholu's 3×3 grid using Rani's clues: eraser top right, pencil top left, apple at row 2 col 2, water bottle at row 3 col 2 (ball already placed at row 1 col 1).
Follow Mini's moves on the 4×4 grid (4 steps right; then 2 left, 1 up); mark Mini's final position; identify what object Jagat thought of.
Play the treasure hunt game with a partner on the 4×4 grid; give and follow step-direction clues to locate the chosen object.

homework.description: From the starting point, trace paths to the flower and count steps for each path; determine whether mango or orange is reachable in fewer steps.

time_bands.activity: Students translate Rani's verbal clues into placements on Bholu's 3×3 grid — Grid Game activity, p.29 ("fill Bholu's 3×3 grid using Rani's clues: eraser top right, pencil top left...."). After completing the grid individually, students share how they decided where 'row 2, column 2' falls, cementing the row-column address idea.

The class works through Treasure Hunt example, p.30 ("follow Mini's moves on the 4×4 grid — 4 steps right; then 2 left, 1 up...."), tracing each move step by step and marking Mini's landing position. Students then name the object found and discuss why the number of steps taken and their direction both matter.

In pairs, students play Treasure Hunt partner game, p.31 ("play the treasure hunt game with a partner on the 4×4 grid; give and follow step-direction clues...."), taking turns as hider and finder. The unit closes with partners sharing one clue sequence they found tricky and explaining how they resolved it.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is counting the starting cell as a step — make sure students understand that a step means moving to the next cell, not staying put. Treasure Hunt path questions, p.31 is set as home practice so students have unhurried time to trace and count multiple paths.
materials: Squared paper for extra grid practice if needed

section_titles: Drone Around the School — Aerial Top View
Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
periods.activity_title: From Drone's Eye to School Map

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Drone Around the School activity, p.31
tasks_in_class.description: Circle the places or things visible in the drone top-view photograph of the school; write their names.
Trace the path from Grade 4 classroom to the stage on the school map; count how many routes you can find.
Identify which traced route is the shortest and explain how you know.

time_bands.activity: Students examine the drone top-view photograph on page 31 — Drone Around the School activity, p.31 ("circle the places or things visible in the drone top-view photograph....") — circling and naming features they recognise. Pairs share observations and discuss why some things look unfamiliar from above, connecting this directly to the top-view idea practised earlier with the brick and matchbox buildings.

Students turn to the school sight map on page 32 and work through Sight Map Q1, p.32 ("trace the path from Grade 4 classroom to the stage; count how many routes you can find...."), drawing each route in a different colour. The class compiles the total number of distinct routes found before moving on.

Students tackle Sight Map Q2, p.32 ("identify which traced route is the shortest and explain how you know...."), comparing their coloured paths and articulating — orally and in writing — their reasoning for calling one route shorter than another.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often pick a route because it 'looks' direct without checking whether it passes through fewer rooms or turns — press them to explain their reasoning rather than simply pointing. The drone photograph is the bridge from single-object top views to a top view of an entire outdoor space; naming that connection aloud helps students see the map as a special kind of top view.
materials: Coloured pencils (at least two colours per student)

section_titles: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
periods.activity_title: Writing Routes, Drawing Your Own School Map

tasks_in_class.description: The water delivery man turned left from the entrance — write directions to help him reach the MDM Kitchen.
Rajat is unwell — choose the best route from the library to the medical room and describe it.
Trace Bholu's path (playground to IT room) and Rani's path (playground to sports room); compare which path is longer.
Draw a sight map showing the route from your school entrance to your classroom and any other important places.

time_bands.activity: Students work through Sight Map Q3, p.32 ("the water delivery man turned left from the entrance — write directions to help him reach the MDM Kitchen....") and Sight Map Q4, p.32 ("Rajat is unwell — choose the best route from the library to the medical room...."), writing out step-by-step directional instructions. Pairs exchange their written directions and test whether a classmate can trace the correct path from the description alone.

Students trace both paths for Sight Map Q5, p.32 ("trace Bholu's path to the IT room and Rani's path to the sports room; compare which is longer....") on their maps and write a sentence comparing path lengths, practising the language of comparison built up across the map tasks.

Students begin and complete Let Us Do (Project Work), p.33 ("draw a sight map showing the route from your school entrance to your classroom...."), sketching the layout, labelling rooms, and marking a clear path. Finished maps are displayed briefly so students can see how different classmates chose to represent the same space.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write directions that make sense to them but are ambiguous for a reader — push them to name landmarks ('turn left at the library') rather than just 'go straight'. The sight map project should start and finish within this unit; students who need more detail can add labels rather than redrawing.
materials: Plain paper or grid paper for the sight map project

periods.activity_title: Hide and Seek: Bringing the Whole Chapter Together

time_bands.activity: The teacher places a common object (a mug or box) on the desk and asks three students to sketch what they see from different positions — above, in front, and from the side. The class identifies each sketch's view name and discusses why all three sketches look different, revisiting the core idea that the observer's position determines the shape seen.

Working in pairs, one student draws a 4×4 grid on paper and secretly places a small object token at any cell; the partner must locate it by asking questions answered only with row-column addresses or step-direction moves ('move 2 right, 1 up'). After two rounds, pairs reflect on which description — row-column address or step sequence — was easier to use and why.

Each student draws a quick top-view map of an imaginary small town with at least four named buildings, marks a starting point and a destination, and writes a set of step-direction instructions guiding a friend from start to finish. Students exchange maps and follow each other's instructions, marking the final landing point; they check whether the destination matches and discuss what made some instructions clearer than others.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the three strands of the chapter — views of objects, row-column position, and map reading — so that students can see them as expressions of a single spatial idea: where you stand and how you describe it. Watch for students who are fluent with grid addresses but write vague map directions; prompt them to use the same precision they applied to the grid game.
materials: A mug or small box for the opening demonstration

items.section_title: Boxy Buildings — Building and Drawing Multiple Views
items.prompt: Priya stacks two boxes — one large box at the bottom and one small box on top. She looks straight down from above. What shape does she see? Draw or describe it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She sees the top face of the small box — a rectangle (or square if the small box is square). Only the top surface of the upper box is visible from directly above.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Picture the top face of the highest object; everything below is hidden from the top view.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student stack two actual boxes and look down; stretch: ask what changes if the large box were on top.

exercise.description: Collect empty matchboxes or boxes; build different buildings; draw their top, side, and front views; challenge friends to match drawing to building.

items.section_title: Drone Around the School — Aerial Top View
items.prompt: A drone flies directly above a school and takes a photograph looking straight down. Which of the following would appear in that photograph?

options.label: A
options.text: The front door of the school building

options.label: B
options.text: The notice board hanging inside the corridor

options.label: C
options.text: The roof of the school building

options.label: D
options.text: The windows on the side wall

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The roof of the school building — it is the surface facing upward and visible from directly above.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A top view shows only the surfaces that face directly upward; vertical or interior surfaces are not visible.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is thinking of the front view rather than the top view.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is thinking of a side view, not a top-down photograph.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not distinguished between what is visible from outside above and what is indoors.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student look down at a flat book placed on the desk and describe what they see; stretch: ask what a drone photograph of a playground would show.

exercise.book_ref: Drone Around the School activity, p.31
exercise.description: Circle the places or things visible in the drone top-view photograph of the school; write their names.

items.section_title: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
items.prompt: Draw a simple top-view map of your classroom. Mark the door, at least two windows, and the teacher's desk. Label each one.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A correctly oriented rectangle representing the classroom, with a gap or labelled rectangle for the door, smaller rectangles or marks for windows on appropriate walls, and a rectangle labelled 'Teacher's desk' near the front. Labels are readable and placed on the correct features.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A sight map is a top-view drawing that labels real locations to help others understand the space.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student look around the room and point to each feature before drawing; stretch: ask the student to add a path from the door to their own desk and write two-step directions for it.

exercise.description: Draw a sight map showing the route from your school entrance to your classroom and any other important places.

items.section_title: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
items.prompt: Three children look at the same cylindrical water bottle — Anil from directly above, Bina from the front, and Charu from the side. Bina and Charu's drawings look the same (a tall rectangle). Anil's drawing looks different. What does Anil's drawing look like?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A circle — looking straight down at the top of a cylinder shows only the circular top face.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify which face of the object is visible from the given position; the top view of a cylinder is its circular top face.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is applying the front or side view to the top position, not thinking about which face faces upward.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be confusing a cylinder with a cone or guessing without reasoning about the shape.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recognises a non-rectangular shape is expected but selects a four-sided figure rather than the circular top.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student look down at a circular bottle cap to confirm what they see; stretch: ask what the top view of a cone would look like and how it differs.

exercise.description: Mini, Bholu and Rani drew the same brick differently — discuss why; fill table: whose drawing shows top view, front view, side view.

items.section_title: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
items.prompt: A pyramid has a square base and four triangular faces. Kezia looks at the pyramid from the front. Raju looks at it from directly above. Whose drawing will show a triangle? Explain why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Kezia's drawing will show a triangle — looking at a pyramid from the front reveals one triangular face as the visible outline. Raju's top view shows the square base with lines going to the centre point.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify which face or outline is visible from the observer's position; the front face of a pyramid is triangular.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a paper pyramid and look at it from each direction before writing; stretch: ask what the side view of the same pyramid looks like and whether it differs from the front view.

exercise.description: Match the side/front/top view drawings made by Jagat and Rani with the correct 3D objects (pyramid, cube, prism/wedge).

items.section_title: Cat Finds Jagat — Row and Column Positions
items.prompt: In a classroom grid with 3 rows and 4 columns, the teacher places a red flag at the desk in row 2, column 3. She then moves it 1 row down and 1 column to the left. Where is the red flag now?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 3, column 2 — starting at row 2 col 3, moving 1 row down reaches row 3; moving 1 column left from col 3 reaches col 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply each move separately: add 1 to the row number for 'down', subtract 1 from the column number for 'left'.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student moved down correctly but added 1 to the column instead of subtracting, confusing left and right.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student moved the column correctly but did not move the row, missing the downward shift.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student moved in the opposite row direction (up instead of down), reversing the row move.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a hand-drawn 3×4 grid and physically move a counter; stretch: ask the student to find all the desks reachable from row 2 col 3 in exactly two moves.

exercise.description: Mark Jagat's position (3rd desk, 1st row); describe position of blue bag; identify object at middle desk of 2nd row; locate notebook; draw an apple at 3rd desk of 2nd row.

items.prompt: On a 4×4 grid, Asha starts at the bottom-left corner. She moves 3 steps right, then 2 steps up. Mark her final position on the grid below and write which row and column she has reached.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Asha reaches column 4, row 3 (counting rows upward from row 1 at the bottom). Starting at column 1 row 1, 3 steps right → column 4; 2 steps up → row 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count each step as moving to the next cell in the given direction; track column and row changes separately.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the grid and move a pencil tip one cell at a time, counting aloud; stretch: ask what sequence of moves would bring Asha back to the starting corner in exactly 5 steps.

exercise.description: Follow Mini's moves on the 4×4 grid (4 steps right; then 2 left, 1 up); mark Mini's final position; identify what object Jagat thought of.

items.section_title: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
items.prompt: Look at this simple school map. The library is at the top-left and the science room is at the bottom-right. Manu finds two different paths from the library to the science room. Path P goes through the hall; Path Q goes through the garden. Path P takes 8 steps and Path Q takes 6 steps. Which path is shorter, and how do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Path Q is shorter because it takes only 6 steps, which is fewer than Path P's 8 steps. Fewer steps means less distance to travel.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the step counts of both paths; the path with the smaller count is the shorter route.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: encourage the student to write the two numbers side by side and circle the smaller one before writing a sentence; stretch: ask what path the student would recommend if the garden were closed and why.

exercise.description: Identify which traced route is the shortest and explain how you know.

items.section_title: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
items.prompt: The milk delivery van enters the school gate and turns right. It needs to reach the kitchen, which is at the end of the second corridor on the left. Write the step-by-step directions you would give the driver.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A correct answer gives a sequence such as: 'Enter the gate, turn right, go straight along the main corridor, take the second turn on the left, the kitchen is at the end of that corridor.' The exact wording may vary; what matters is a clear sequence of turns and landmarks.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the map to trace the route step by step, naming each turn direction and a landmark to confirm each move.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace the route with a finger and say each step aloud before writing; stretch: ask the student to write a second, alternative route and compare the number of turns each requires.

exercise.description: The water delivery man turned left from the entrance — write directions to help him reach the MDM Kitchen.

items.section_title: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
items.prompt: The picture on p.26 shows an everyday object drawn from one position. The drawing is a perfect circle. Which view of the object is shown?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Top view — a circle as the outline is the top face of a cylindrical or circular object seen from directly above.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the shape of the outline to the face that would be visible from the named position.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not connected a circular outline to the top position; they may think the front can show a circle for any object.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is guessing between side and top without using the circular shape as evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is not using the view name systematically; 'back view' is not one of the three positions studied.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a round lid and ask them to look at it from above, then from the front; stretch: ask which everyday objects would show a circle from the front view instead of the top.

exercise.description: Look at nine pictures of objects (TV, sofa, slipper, cup, school bus, chair, bolt, pizza cutter, helmet); write each object's name and which view is shown.

items.section_title: Grid Game — Describing Positions on a Grid
items.prompt: On a 3×3 grid, a pencil is placed at row 1, column 3 (top-right corner). A sharpener is placed at row 3, column 1 (bottom-left corner). Which cell is at the exact centre of the grid?
items.visual_stimulus: number_line: Row 1 Col 1 | Row 1 Col 2 | Row 1 Col 3 | Row 2 Col 1 | Row 2 Col 2 | Row 2 Col 3 | Row 3 Col 1 | Row 3 Col 2 | Row 3 Col 3

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 2, column 2 — the middle row is row 2 and the middle column is column 2; their intersection is the centre cell.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In a 3×3 grid, the middle row and middle column both have index 2; their intersection is the centre.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student identified the correct column but anchored to the first row rather than the middle row.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identified the correct row but anchored to the first column rather than the middle column.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have confused corner and centre, or is guessing without applying the row-column system.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the 3×3 grid and cross out row 1, row 3, col 1, col 3 to find what remains; stretch: ask what happens to the centre cell if the grid grows to 5×5.

exercise.description: Fill Bholu's 3×3 grid using Rani's clues: eraser top right, pencil top left, apple at row 2 col 2, water bottle at row 3 col 2 (ball already placed at row 1 col 1).
